lesson.title: How strongly buyers respond

steps.headline: Elasticity compares how far quantity moves with how far price moved.

lead.text: Price elasticity of demand divides the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price. Each percentage uses the average of the two values as its base: the midpoint method.
Above 1, demand is elastic. Below 1, it is inelastic.

steps.headline: A gym's price rises from £4 to £6 a visit and visits fall from 130 to 70 a day. What is the elasticity of demand?

workedSteps.text: Quantity change as a share of the average quantity.
Price change as a share of the average price.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.

steps.headline: A bus pass falls from £6 to £4 and passes sold rise from 95 to 105. What is the elasticity of demand?

workedSteps.text: The average quantity is 100 and the quantity changes by 10.
The average price is £5 and the price changes by £2.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.

reveal.text: Elasticity of 3 is well above 1: demand for tickets is elastic, so buyers respond more than in proportion.

lead.text: Same method, a different market. Average first, then divide the two percentage changes.

steps.headline: Elastic demand: a price cut raises revenue. Inelastic demand: it lowers it.

lead.text: Revenue is price times quantity. A price cut shrinks the first and grows the second. If quantity grows by a bigger percentage than price fell, revenue rises. If it grows by less, revenue falls.

reveal.text: Revenue rose from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, as the rule says for elastic demand.

lead.text: Back to the concert: the price fell from £11 to £9 and sales rose from 35 to 65. Work out the revenue at each price.

reveal.text: Revenue is £990 at both prices, so elasticity here is exactly 1. On a straight line demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low ones, and revenue peaks where it equals 1.

lead.text: A straight demand line has a different elasticity at each price. Test a museum, with demand Qd = 200 − 10P, as its entry price falls.

lesson.orientation: Measure price elasticity of demand with the midpoint method and predict what a price change does to revenue.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A food stall wonders whether a lower price will bring in more money.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how strongly buyers respond to price, and say what a price change does to revenue.

recap.keyIdea: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity over the percentage change in price, taken at the midpoint. Elastic demand means a price cut raises revenue; inelastic demand means it lowers it.

blocks.text: You measured 1.5 for gym visits, 0.25 for bus passes and 3 for concert tickets. At the museum, revenue stayed at £990 when elasticity was exactly 1.

recap.nextHook: Elasticity shows how buyers react. Next: what buyers and sellers gain from a trade.

questions.prompt: When the price of a concert ticket falls from £11 to £9, the number sold rises from 35 to 65. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
hints: Divide the change in quantity by the average of the two quantities.
Divide the change in price by the average of the two prices.
Divide the first percentage by the second and drop the sign.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Quantity changed by 60% of its average, price by 20% of its average: 60 ÷ 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides price by quantity. Put the quantity percentage on top.
That is the change in quantity, not the elasticity. Express it as a share of the average first.
Check your base: use the average of the two quantities, 50, not an end value.

questions.prompt: Ticket sales rise from 35 at £11 to 65 at £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
Compute revenue at each price.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue goes from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, a rise of £200.

questions.onCorrect: £200 more. Elastic demand means the gain in quantity outweighs the cut in price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue before the cut. Subtract it from the revenue after.
That is the revenue after the cut. Subtract the revenue before.
That is the price cut. Revenue is price times quantity at each price.

hints: Use the average quantity as the base for the quantity change.
Use the average price as the base for the price change.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 0.25. The quantity percentage is much smaller than the price percentage, so demand is inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
That is the quantity percentage alone. Divide it by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: Museum demand is Qd = 200 − 10P. The entry price falls from £11 to £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Find the quantity at each price.
Multiply each price by its quantity.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Visits rise from 90 to 110; revenue is 11 × 90 = £990 before and 9 × 110 = £990 after, so it does not change.

questions.onCorrect: None. Revenue is the same at both prices, which is what unit elasticity looks like.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue at one price. Compare it with the revenue at the other.
That is the price fall, not the change in revenue.

questions.prompt: Demand for a firm's product is inelastic. The firm raises its price. What happens to its total revenue?
hints: Compare the percentage change in price with the percentage change in quantity.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so price times quantity goes up.

questions.onCorrect: It rises. With inelastic demand quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the two percentage changes: which one is bigger when demand is inelastic?
Revenue stays level only at unit elasticity. Here quantity responds by less than price.

questions.prompt: The price of a phone case rises from £8 to £12 and quantity demanded falls from 110 to 90. Find the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand.
hints: Average the two quantities and the two prices.
Express each change as a share of its average.
Divide the quantity share by the price share.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5. A 20% change in quantity against a 40% change in price: inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Put the quantity percentage on top.
That is the quantity percentage alone. Divide it by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: A food stall cuts the price of a snack from £5 to £4 and sells 90 a day instead of 60. By how many pounds do its daily takings change?
hints: Takings are price times number sold.
Work out the takings at each price.
Subtract the old takings from the new.
questions.onCorrect: £60 more. The extra snacks sold more than made up for the pound lost on each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the extra snacks sold. Takings are price times quantity at each price.
That is the takings after the cut. Compare them with the takings before.
That is the takings before the cut. Compare them with the takings after.

questions.prompt: A price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 30%. Is demand elastic or inelastic?

choices.label: Elastic: quantity responds more than in proportion.
Inelastic: quantity responds less than in proportion.

acceptedIdeas: Elastic: quantity responds more than in proportion.

hints: Divide the quantity change by the price change.
questions.onCorrect: Elastic. 30% ÷ 10% is 3, above 1: quantity moved by more than price did.

misconceptions.feedback: Inelastic means quantity moves by less than price. Here it moved by more.
The percentages only match at exactly 1. Divide one by the other to see.

questions.prompt: Why divide by the average quantity, not by 130?

choices.label: So the percentage is the same whichever way the price moves.
Because the old figure is unreliable.
Because the average is easier to calculate.

acceptedIdeas: So the percentage is the same whichever way the price moves.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rise from one value to another and a fall back would give different percentages without a common base. The average is the same both ways.

hints: What would happen if the price went back up?
questions.onCorrect: One shared base means a rise and a fall between the same two points give the same elasticity.

misconceptions.feedback: The old figure is fine. The issue is that a rise and a fall between the same values would give different percentages.
It is slightly harder, not easier. The point is consistency.

questions.prompt: Quantity change as a percentage of the average, 10 on an average of 100
hints: Divide the change by the average, not by an end value.
The average is given in the line above.
Divide ten by one hundred and write it as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 10%: the change divided by the average quantity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share as a decimal. Write it as a percentage.
That is the average, not the change as a share of it.

questions.prompt: A good's price elasticity of demand is 0.4. The seller cuts its price. What happens to total revenue?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Elasticity below 1 means inelastic: quantity rises by a smaller percentage than price falls, so revenue falls.

questions.onCorrect: It falls. With inelastic demand the price cut costs more than the extra sales bring in.

misconceptions.feedback: Revenue rises after a cut only when elasticity is above 1. Compare 0.4 with 1.
Revenue stays level only when elasticity is exactly 1.

questions.prompt: Demand for a medicine is inelastic. Its price rises from £10 to £12 and sales fall from 100 to 95 a day. By how many pounds does daily revenue change?
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
Work out the revenue at each price.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.
questions.onCorrect: £140 more. Inelastic demand: sales barely fell, so the higher price lifted revenue.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue after the rise. Subtract the revenue before it.
That is the revenue before the rise. Compare it with the revenue after.
That is the price rise. Revenue is price times quantity at each price.
